editorial.summary: Estevan Oriol joins David Choe, Asa Akira, Money Mark, Critter, Valentin, and Bobby Namba. The episode opens with Asa's AVN Female Performer of the Year speech and then makes naming its first serious subject: Estevan explains that he was born Estevan Heriberto Oriol, that his mother changed his first name to Steve after discrimination at school, and that he later reclaimed Estevan even though institutions continue to return Devin or Esteban. The ASR repeatedly reproduces the very erasure being discussed, so the correction layer follows the E-S-T-E-V-A-N spelling he supplies. The group then revisits the Turkey, Cappadocia, Afghanistan, and Dubai trip. Estevan describes salvaging travel after Afghanistan initially fell through; David supplies danger near-misses, Critter's visual acuity, calligraphy and meat-market visits, expatriate life, gender restrictions, drug use, and food. These remain individual travel accounts, not comprehensive reporting about Afghanistan. A long organ-donation argument contrasts bodily autonomy, saving unknown lives, a parent's grief, Buddhist family ritual, uncertain religious claims, and Japanese cremation bone-picking. Febreze's advertising history becomes a theory of reward cues, which David maps onto bedtime habits and masturbation. Valentin then discusses a year-long private relationship, fidelity, pregnancy, marriage, work, and a very large Mexican family. The room idealizes his calm answers while also confronting secrecy and risk; private partners and relatives remain unindexed. Work becomes the second center. David praises runners, assistants, exceptional late-night restaurant service, and people who act as if the current task is their real job. He contrasts refusing routine tips with claims of giving $100 at IHOP and $6,000 at Carrows, then repeats Jane Choe's distinction between working hard and working smart. The record keeps these transactions attributed and maps their tension with status, service labor, deservingness, and David's demand for total attention. Drug stories move from fake cocaine made with Splenda to OxyContin, “Cold Turkey,” Tom Ford Tuscan Leather, and a pseudonymous rehab peer. David describes the peer with lay psychiatric labels, engineers a reconciliation through a hug, then retaliates against another humiliation by defecating in the man's luggage. The editorial layer preserves conduct and contradiction without diagnosing or identifying the patient. Dolphin-assisted activity follows as spiritual testimony, not clinical treatment. A fan-owned frozen-yogurt shop, Pizzanista!, Bobby and Carol, bodily privacy, sexual embarrassment, and private friends lead into trivia on “The Lady in Red” and O.A.R.'s “On My Way.” Seven empty cleaner drops are safe; forty-seven contextual decisions materially improve retrieval; 3,297 identity windows are intact and named dialogue remains withheld.
